comparisons.peer_summary: AMD relies on third-party manufacturers, primarily TSMC for advanced nodes and GLOBALFOUNDRIES for larger nodes, as well as ATMP partners, without long-term commitment contracts for all services, creating risks of supply constraints, capacity prioritization for competitors, and price increases.
comparisons.comparison: Both QCOM and AMD highlight the risk that their reliance on third-party foundries may lead to insufficient capacity to meet customer demand. QCOM discloses that its ability to meet increased demand is limited by the inability to obtain necessary manufacturing and test capacity, while AMD explicitly states that if TSMC cannot manufacture sufficient quantities of wafers for their products, it would have a material adverse effect on their business. Both companies identify supply constraints at key manufacturing partners as a primary driver for failing to fulfill market demand.

sentences.text: Our ability to meet increased demand for our products has been in the past and may in the future be limited due to the inability to obtain the additional manufacturing, assembly and test capacity necessary to fully meet such demand.

For example, if TSMC is not able to manufacture wafers for our microprocessor and GPU products at 7 nm or smaller nodes and our newest IC products in sufficient quantities to meet customer demand, it could have a material adverse effect on our business.

comparisons.peer_topic: Manufacturing Capacity, Yields, and Demand Forecasting Risks
comparisons.peer_summary: The company faces risks from inaccurate customer demand estimates and the inability to maintain appropriate manufacturing capacity and yields, which could result from insufficient expansion investments, overestimation of demand leading to excess capacity, or reduced yields from design or manufacturing issues.
comparisons.comparison: QCOM and AVGO both disclose risks associated with the inability to secure sufficient manufacturing capacity or yield performance to meet customer needs. QCOM notes that transitions to new process technology nodes drive product cost increases, while AVGO warns that failure to adjust manufacturing to meet demand, or reduced yields due to design or manufacturing issues, could cause delays in supplying products and result in lost sales. Both companies link these operational constraints directly to negative impacts on results of operations.

sentences.text: We expect transitions to new generations of leading process technology nodes to continue to drive product cost increases from certain of our key semiconductor wafer suppliers, which may negatively impact our margins.

Our ability to meet increased demand for our products has been in the past and may in the future be limited due to the inability to obtain the additional manufacturing, assembly and test capacity necessary to fully meet such demand.

Similarly, reduced product yields, due to design or manufacturing issues or otherwise, may involve significant time and cost to remedy and cause delays in our ability to supply product to our customers, all of which could cause us to forgo sales, incur liabilities or lose customers, and harm our results of operations.

Conversely, if we overestimate customer demand, we would experience excess capacity and fixed costs at these facilities will not be fully absorbed, which could adversely affect our results of operations.

comparisons.peer_topic: Global supply chain complexity and disruption risks
comparisons.peer_summary: Intel's complex global supply chain is susceptible to disruptions from supplier capacity constraints, quality issues, cyberattacks, and natural disasters, which can increase costs, delay shipments, and harm financial results.
comparisons.comparison: Both QCOM and INTC identify supplier capacity constraints as a specific mechanism that disrupts operations and hinders the ability to meet customer delivery obligations. QCOM states that inability to obtain additional manufacturing capacity limits their ability to meet increased demand, while INTC lists 'suppliers extending lead times, experiencing capacity constraints, [and] allocating supply to other customers' as key supply chain issues that prevent meeting customer demand. Both frame this as a direct threat to their operational fulfillment capabilities.

sentences.text: Our ability to meet increased demand for our products has been in the past and may in the future be limited due to the inability to obtain the additional manufacturing, assembly and test capacity necessary to fully meet such demand.

▪suppliers extending lead times, experiencing capacity constraints, limiting or canceling supply, allocating supply to other customers including competitors, delaying or canceling deliveries, or increasing prices;

These and other supply chain issues can increase our costs, disrupt or reduce our production, delay our product shipments, prevent us from meeting customer demand, damage our customer relationships, or negatively affect our reputation.

comparisons.peer_topic: Supply chain dependency and material availability
comparisons.peer_summary: The supply chain depends on third-party providers and exacting material standards, with limited sources for certain components. Shortages of raw materials, chemicals, or silicon wafers, along with inflationary pressures and lack of long-term capacity commitments in contracts, may limit bit shipments, increase costs, or disrupt operations. Additionally, reliance on China for rare earth elements poses a risk if exports are restricted.
comparisons.comparison: QCOM and MU both disclose that constraints in supply chain capacity can directly limit their ability to deliver products and harm financial results. QCOM explains that inability to obtain additional manufacturing capacity limits its ability to meet increased demand, while MU states that constraints for certain materials and components could limit bit shipments, having a material adverse effect on business. Both identify the limitation of physical supply capacity as a critical bottleneck for revenue generation.

sentences.text: Our ability to meet increased demand for our products has been in the past and may in the future be limited due to the inability to obtain the additional manufacturing, assembly and test capacity necessary to fully meet such demand.

Constraints within our supply chain for certain materials and integrated circuit components could limit our bit shipments, which could have a material adverse effect on our business, results of operations, or financial condition.

comparisons.peer_topic: Third-party supply chain dependencies and risks
comparisons.peer_summary: Nvidia depends on third-party suppliers, foundries, and subcontractors for manufacturing, assembly, testing, and procurement, lacking its own capabilities in these areas. This dependency reduces control over quantity, quality, yields, and delivery schedules. Risks include lack of guaranteed supply, foundry capacity failures, geographic concentration, supplier loss, quality failures, shipment delays, and natural disaster disruptions, which could adversely affect business operations, gross margin, and financial results.
comparisons.comparison: Both QCOM and NVDA emphasize the risks inherent in relying on third-party foundries for advanced process technology transitions. QCOM warns that transitions to new leading process technology nodes drive product cost increases which may negatively impact margins. Similarly, NVDA highlights the risk of foundries failing to successfully implement high-quality process technologies, including transitions to smaller geometry nodes, which can affect their ability to meet demand and scale supply. Both link technological transition risks at foundries to supply and cost challenges.
